items.title: Barry Kernfeld interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, December 16, 2020
items.q: over my shoulder I have Count Basie and Lester Young and I think of them as playing, I guess, functional music.

ctx.x: role. This is functional music, this is culture, this is social interrelationships. And to see that was just an eye opening experience for an 18-year-old kid who grew up in Jewish culture you know. It was fantastic. And I think there are many other anecdotal instant answers like that of just experiencing life in ways in which musics of African-American origin had a cultural meaning that I didn’t find elsewhere. It wasn’t a split between music and life. I think another component of the answer that can go down a…

Okay. Well the more we talk the more I think we have in common, because I had a similar experience in growing up in Rochester with the kind of thing you’re describing so I thank you for sharing that with me. You used the word “functional.” And over my shoulder I have Count Basie and Lester Young and I think of them as playing, I guess, functional music. I mean people could dance to it, they took joy in it, it hit their solar plexuses perhaps more than their head. I’m not sure that’s the way to put it but, so I’m…

Well I don’t see how there could be because popular tastes have changed several times from the years in which, from the decades in which jazz was the functional music for American society. It was rock. It was hip hop. It was disco. Those are out of order, but it was a whole bunch of things. Rock & roll, since that era, and that’s just practical what people like to do to hang out, what they like to listen to. Now it’s not even live music anymore. What people like to listen to is DJs.
